enrichment.short_title: Bob Marley royalties strike-out application refused
key_facts: Aston Barrett sued Universal-Island and UMG for royalties, copyright and performers' rights over Bob Marley and the Wailers recordings made under 1974 and 1975 recording agreements.

The defendants and Marley adult beneficiaries applied to strike out the claim or obtain summary judgment, arguing the 1994 Settlement Agreement and with-prejudice dismissal of earlier New York proceedings barred further litigation.
The court held Carlton Barrett's estate was not bound by the 1994 settlement and that Aston Barrett could continue as administrator of his brother's estate.
Despite strong suspicion the defendants would prevail at trial, the claims were too complex and factually disputed for summary determination after a four-day hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in the Chancery Division for strike-out and summary judgment on claims for royalties, copyright, performers' rights and unjust enrichment, with applications to add Marley beneficiaries as defendants and Part 20 claimants.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants' applications for strike out and summary judgment dismissed; Aston Barrett permitted to continue in personal capacity and as administrator of Carlton Barrett's estate.
enrichment.ratio: Even where abuse-of-process and settlement-release arguments appear strong, strike-out or summary judgment under CPR Parts 3.4 and 24.2 requires high confidence without a mini-trial; where issues are complex and a full trial is likely in any event, the court may exercise its discretion to allow weak-looking claims to proceed, especially where claims on behalf of a non-party estate are not barred by prior settlements.
legal_issues: Whether the 1994 Settlement Agreement barred Aston Barrett's current claims
Whether issue estoppel arose from the with-prejudice dismissal of the 1989 New York Action
Whether the Barretts were parties to the 1974 and 1975 recording agreements
Ownership of copyright in six compositions and performers' rights claims
Appropriateness of summary disposal where the application itself becomes a mini-trial

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors negligence permission to appeal tanker claim
key_facts: Somatra recovered over $5 million from solicitors SRT after alleging breach of duty in litigation over loss of a tanker caused them to settle for 66⅔% rather than 75% or full value.
Morison J found SRT partner Mr Williams breached duty in several respects, including dishonesty over expert instructions and client meetings with the bank.
SRT sought permission to appeal findings on two further alleged breaches and on causation linking loss of confidence to acceptance of the lower settlement.

The Court of Appeal granted permission on several points including settlement authority, causation, remoteness, and the judge's trial-outcome findings, but refused permission on one dishonesty finding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral application for permission to appeal from a High Court judgment awarding damages for solicitor negligence, with directions on security for stay and skeleton length.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on most contested issues; permission refused on challenge to finding that Mr Williams lied about inviting lay clients to a meeting; stay conditional on bank guarantee.
enrichment.ratio: In a complex solicitor-negligence case where a client settled litigation for less after loss of confidence in its lawyers, arguable questions arise on whether breaches caused acceptance of a lower settlement, whether an underwriter had market authority to offer 75%, and whether loss should be assessed as lost chance rather than by re-trying the underlying claim.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's finding of professional dishonesty on the bank meeting invitation was open on the evidence
Whether conduct at the settlement meeting amounted to breach of solicitor's duty
Causation between breach of duty and acceptance of 66⅔% settlement
Whether Mr Domingo had market authority to settle at 75%
Appropriate measure of loss: full trial outcome versus loss of chance

confidence.notes: Permission judgment with clear issue-by-issue dispositions; no statutory framework central to decision.

enrichment.short_title: Human Rights Act procedure in pending care proceedings
key_facts: Care proceedings concerning a child L began in the family proceedings court after the local authority decided on an adoption care plan.
The mother sought transfer to the High Court to compel the authority to pursue long-term fostering instead of adoption, invoking the Human Rights Act and inherent jurisdiction.
Munby J held the court could not under Part IV or the inherent jurisdiction direct the content of a care plan; relief required judicial review or HRA proceedings.

He gave guidance that Convention challenges arising while care proceedings are on foot should normally be litigated within those proceedings under section 7(1)(b), not by hiving-off separate High Court applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management hearing in the Family Division on the mother's applications under the Human Rights Act 1998 and the inherent jurisdiction challenging an adoption care plan, with procedural guidance endorsed by the President.
enrichment.outcome: Procedural guidance given; whole care proceedings retained in the Family Division for final hearing because the case would not be ready in the FPC in time.
enrichment.ratio: Where care proceedings are pending, Human Rights Act complaints about a local authority's care plan or decision-making should normally be raised within those proceedings under section 7(1)(b) HRA 1998 by the court hearing the care case; separate free-standing HRA applications or split hearings in the High Court are inappropriate save in wholly exceptional cases, and the inherent jurisdiction cannot compel a public authority's care-plan discretion.
legal_issues: Whether the High Court can compel a local authority to change its care plan
Relationship between Part IV Children Act jurisdiction, inherent jurisdiction, judicial review and HRA remedies
Appropriate forum for article 8 challenges during pending care proceedings
Whether FPC or County Court can determine Convention issues in care cases
index_terms: Inner London and City Family Proceedings Court

linked_authorities.name: Re S and D (Children: Powers of Court)
In re S (Minors) (Care Order: Implementation of Care Plan)

confidence.notes: Authoritative procedural judgment with President's endorsement; substantive care merits expressly not decided.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair hearing on child removal from jurisdiction
key_facts: A 2000 county court order required both parents' written consent before removing child IHM from the jurisdiction, save for short Scotland visits by the father.
Three years later the father applied to vary the order because mutual vetoes had made the arrangement unworkable.
Judge Morton Jack dismissed the application as misconceived and ordered the litigant-in-person father to pay £950 costs without hearing his evidence.
The Court of Appeal set aside that order, found the father had not received a fair hearing, and approved a consent variation allowing 28-day foreign holidays except to Jamaica.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission to appeal granted at outset; appeal from county court order dismissing father's application to vary a restriction on removing a child from the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Morton Jack J's order set aside; Callman J's order varied by consent to permit holidays abroad up to 28 days with passport arrangements; Jamaica excluded unless further court order.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant in person is entitled to a fair hearing on the merits of an application to vary a restrictive child-abroad order; where the judge misconceived the issue, failed to hear evidence, and treated the application as solely about one past holiday, the resulting dismissal and costs order cannot stand.
legal_issues: Fair treatment of litigants in person in family applications
Whether continuing restrictions on removing a child from the jurisdiction remained necessary
Appropriateness of costs orders where the court misunderstood the application
Risk-based exclusion of travel to a non-Hague Convention country

confidence.notes: Short procedural fairness judgment with agreed replacement order; limited statutory citation in source.

enrichment.short_title: Sheep carcase disposal case stated appeal allowed
key_facts: A farmer was prosecuted for failing without undue delay to dispose of sheep carcases found on remote grazing land during the 2001 foot and mouth crisis.
Selby justices dismissed three summonses on no case to answer, holding expert evidence on date of death and husbandry was required and the farmer's unawareness was not culpable.
On case stated, Goldring J held possession or control did not require knowledge, photographs showed two-to-three-day-old carcases, and undue delay was a question of fact capable of proof.
The case was remitted to the magistrates; the defendant's costs order was set aside and he was ordered to pay £2,000 appeal costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' no-case-to-answer ruling in a prosecution under the Animal By-Products Order 1999.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to Selby Justices on three charges; magistrates' costs order set aside; respondent ordered to pay £2,000 appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: In a prosecution under article 5(1) of the Animal By-Products Order 1999, the prosecution need only prove the carcase was on land in the defendant's possession or control and that disposal was delayed without undue delay; knowledge is not required, expert evidence on date of death is not mandatory where photographs suffice, and a reasonable bench could find a case to answer where carcases had been present for two to three days.
legal_issues: Meaning of possession or control under article 5(1)
Meaning of without undue delay
Whether prosecution must prove actual or constructive knowledge
Need for expert evidence on date of death
Use of photographs as evidence of carcase age

linked_authorities.name: Northumberland County Council Trading Standards Department v George Foster Stephenson

confidence.notes: Clear case-stated answers on possession, delay and evidential threshold.

enrichment.short_title: Labour Party candidate imposition injunction refused

statutes_considered.title: Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000

key_facts: Six Labour-selected Nottingham city council candidates challenged the NEC's decision to rule their ward selections unsound after investigation into membership abuse and vote rigging.
The Party refused nomination certificates and sought to impose alternative candidates before the May 2003 local elections.

Stanley Burnton J refused interim mandatory injunctions requiring the Party to nominate the claimants, holding the NEC likely had power to deselect and impose candidates and that natural-justice flaws were unlikely to succeed.
Claimants could stand as independents; the court should not compel a party to field candidates in whose selection it lacked confidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent interim application for mandatory injunctions and declarations that claimants were lawfully selected Labour candidates for imminent local government elections.
enrichment.outcome: Application for interim relief dismissed; Party permitted to impose alternative candidates and withhold authorised nomination certificates.
enrichment.ratio: On an urgent pre-election application, where a registered political party genuinely believes local candidate selections were corrupted, the court should not grant mandatory injunctions compelling the party to nominate those candidates; contractual NEC powers under Labour Party rules to declare selections unsound and impose candidates are arguable and supported by practice, and trust-based party-candidate relations weigh against coercive relief.
legal_issues: Whether the NEC had power under party rules to deselect and impose local government candidates
Validity of delegation to disputes panel, regional board and investigating panel
Natural justice in internal party investigations
Appropriateness of mandatory injunctions affecting democratic nominations
Effect of delay on interim relief
index_terms: Political Parties Elections and Referendums Act 2000

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage undue influence and half-share sale order

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Mrs Achampong charged the matrimonial home to secure a loan for her husband's cousin's Ghana business; she claimed the charge was procured by her husband's undue influence.
The county court set aside the charge against Mrs Achampong and refused the bank's alternative claim under section 63 LPA 1925 or an order for sale.
The Court of Appeal held the bank was put on inquiry and had not taken reasonable steps under Etridge (No 2) to ensure she understood the transaction, despite solicitors acting for all parties.
The charge remained effective against Mr Achampong's half-share; an order for sale was substituted under TOLATA 1996.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Shoreditch County Court possession and undue-influence proceedings concerning a legal charge over jointly owned property.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part and dismissed in part; first ground dismissed; bank entitled to equitable charge over Mr Achampong's half-share; order for sale substituted; case remitted on practical sale directions.
enrichment.ratio: After Etridge (No 2), a lender put on inquiry by a non-commercial surety relationship cannot rely merely on knowing a solicitor acts for the wife; it must take reasonable steps to ensure she received advice on the transaction's risks. Where a charge is voidable as to the wife but valid as to the husband's share, section 63 LPA 1925 creates an equitable charge over his beneficial interest and TOLATA 1996 may require sale where refusing sale indefinitely prejudices the secured creditor.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Achampong's charge was procured by undue influence
Whether the bank was put on inquiry and took reasonable protective steps
Effect of section 63 LPA 1925 where charge voidable against one co-owner
Exercise of discretion under TOLATA 1996 sections 14 and 15 to order sale

linked_authorities.name: Royal Bank of Scotland plc v Etridge (No 2)
UCB Home Loans Corporation Ltd v Moore
Bank of Ireland Home Mortgages Ltd v Bell

confidence.notes: Detailed post-Etridge analysis with clear split outcome on three grounds of appeal.

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Mr Fox bought open-countryside land in a special landscape area and kept racehorses there with stables, fencing and hardstanding without planning permission.
The council issued an enforcement notice alleging mixed agricultural and horse-keeping use; planning permission for a mixed equestrian/agricultural use was refused.
An Inspector dismissed enforcement and planning appeals, finding horses were kept rather than merely grazed and development harmed the landscape.
Sullivan J rejected five grounds of challenge, holding the Inspector lawfully applied Sykes on grazing versus keeping and properly weighed conservation works and prior intentions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 289 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to an Inspector's dismissal of an enforcement notice appeal by written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Inspector's enforcement decision upheld; appellant ordered to pay Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £3,657.25.
enrichment.ratio: Where an enforcement notice alleges mixed agricultural use and horse keeping, the Inspector may lawfully conclude a material change of use from evidence of supplementary feeding, number of horses and site works; under Sykes the predominant purpose matters, but occasional feeding does not make keeping merely grazing, and an appellant's stated intention to establish mixed use is relevant though not determinative on a ground (b) appeal.
legal_issues: Grazing versus keeping of horses under Sykes
Whether Inspector misapplied predominant-use test
Relevance of racehorse status and breeding activity
Materiality of conservation improvements and public petition
Whether removal of buildings was disproportionate under ground (f)

enrichment.short_title: Director misappropriation summary judgment and tracing

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Bracken Partners brought derivative and direct claims against EGL chairman Mr Gutteridge for misappropriating company funds, including £272,000 used to buy a house registered in his wife's name.
EGL was in compulsory liquidation; Crouch Chapman identified £358,000 in presumed personal payments by the executive chairman without section 317 disclosure.
The court declared Ms Smalley held 39/40ths of the property on trust for EGL, ordered sale, and granted summary judgment for £62,342 after crediting sums tied to the property.
Attempts to deny EGL's tracing claim failed; a failed settlement agreement did not block relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Summary judgment application under CPR Part 24 in Chancery proceedings, including joinder of EGL as claimant in liquidation and proprietary tracing claim over residential property.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted for proprietary declaration, order for sale of property, and money judgment for £62,342; stay on earlier costs order lifted subject to formal application.
enrichment.ratio: Where company funds misappropriated through a brief account transfer are used to buy property in a volunteer recipient's name, the company may trace into the property and obtain a trust declaration without a pre-existing fiduciary relationship with the recipient; an executive director who causes unauthorised personal payments breaches fiduciary duty and cannot rely on set-off against the insolvent company except under strict mutuality rules.
legal_issues: Whether EGL had a proprietary interest traceable into property bought with misappropriated funds
Need for fiduciary relationship before equitable tracing
Treatment of alleged loan and section 330 illegality
Summary judgment on undisputed misappropriation sums
Set-off against company in liquidation

enrichment.short_title: Director's purchase of adjacent mill as corporate opportunity
key_facts: Bhullar Bros Ltd was a family grocery company whose two director families each held 50% of the shares; relations broke down and asset-split negotiations failed.
Directors Inderjit and Jatinderjit Bhullar bought adjacent White Hall Mill through their company Silvercrest without telling co-directors, despite the company's objects including property investment.
The trial judge found a real sensible possibility of conflict and declared Silvercrest held the property on trust for the company at cost, with an account of profits.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding directors in a fiduciary capacity must not exploit commercial opportunities in the company's line of business without full company consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a section 459 unfair prejudice petition judgment granting proprietary relief for breach of fiduciary duty; no cross-appeal on refusal of buy-out relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; declaration that Silvercrest holds White Hall Mill on trust for Bhullar Bros Ltd and order to transfer at purchase price upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A director who, while still serving and while the company remains trading in a line of business including property investment, acquires for personal benefit a commercially attractive adjacent property without disclosure breaches the no-conflict rule in Phipps v Boardman: reasonable persons would see a real sensible possibility of conflict, and the opportunity was information the company was entitled to receive regardless of whether it would have taken it up.
legal_issues: Whether acquisition of White Hall Mill was a maturing business opportunity
Application of the real sensible possibility of conflict test
Whether directors may exploit privately discovered opportunities in the company's line of business
Need for full disclosure and company consent
Constructive trust over property acquired in breach of duty

linked_authorities.name: Industrial Development Consultants Ltd v Cooley

confidence.notes: Leading CA restatement of director conflict principles on undisputed facts; petition buy-out refusal not appealed.
